In real-world scenarios, agents frequently encounter environments characterized by partial observability and dynamic transition rules that are often beyond their control. Experiments on HDPDP applied to a variety of benchmark problems indicate that it successfully recovers the true underlying environment dynamics reward structure more accurately than current state-of-the-art methods when trained on a mixture of heterogeneous trajectories. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that HDPDP exhibits significantly improved sample efficiency by leveraging shared patterns across multiple environments.

Quantization has garnered significant interest as an effective strategy for both speeding up inference and conserving memory in deep learning. While it reliably enhances model efficiency, it previously struggled to consistently maintain accuracy. In this paper, we investigate Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) to analyze why generalization previously proved unstable. Our findings confirm that existing BNNs fail to generalize due to limited expressiveness, a flaw we rigorously demonstrate by analyzing the Binary Neural Network Kernel (NNTK). To resolve this limitation, we propose Normalized Binary Convolution (NBC), a novel quantization scheme grounded in number theoretic insights. Our method ensures symmetry and independence among BNN nodes, thereby facilitating the convergence of expected Hessian information in the large model regime. Beyond improving the generalization stability of BNNs, our work offers rigorous rigors for quantization- induced expressiveness failures across all finite-level approximate numerical schemes. Furthermore, normalization proves universally beneficial in binary architectures, aiding optimization by ensuring stable learning without compromising model capacity or accuracy in a data-efficient manner. Empirical results validate our approach: BC+BN achieves competitive accuracy compared to 8-bit floating point models. Our code will be made publicly available.

Advancements in artificial intelligence have intensified pressure on stakeholders to deploy systems efficiently and effectively. Unfortunately, past AI systems have suffered recurring design flaws that could have been prevented if the source of the error was not time-consuming. To address this, we established the AI Incident Repository: a structured, searchable database intended to help professionals identify preventable past errors and implement corrective measures. The implementation of this system should enable stakeholders to avoid many common mistakes for future AI-designed stakeholders.

The gradient descent precise renormalization group (gdPRG) represents an optimization-driven variant of the renormalization group (RG) method for studying turbulent flows. In this unidirectional RG framework, RG transformations (RGTs) sequentially map turbulent statistics from smaller scales to larger ones; in gdPRG, these transformations are determined optimally by minimizing the time derivative of the effective potential. This potential drives the evolution and signifies the probability measure of observing specific configurations within turbulent fields. Using potential minimization minimizes the estimated RG time derivatives rationally. Consequently, the optimized RGT compresses fields by retaining only significant, persistent structures while filtering out transient small-scale fluctuations. A critical advantage of the gdPRG method lies in its compatibility with finite-size sampling due to the utilization of RG-optimal transformations. Furthermore, because the precise renormalization group traditionally demands extensive datasets—specifically, sampling far exceeding the critical size ($\prec L_c^3$), where $L_c$ denotes coherence length—gdPRG breaks this constraint by functioning effectively even with limited sample volumes.

Out-of-distribution or outlier events are ubiquitous across physical and biological fields, often characterized by extreme magnitude and rarity. For instance, at the cellular level, such outliers encompass the abundance fluctuations of mRNA and protein molecules, as well as the abnormal activity of neurons and T-cells; similarly, they include financial market crashes and the size distribution of typhoons. Despite their prevalence, theoretical understanding remains scarce. In this work, we examine an anisotropic stochastic matrix at a sink, specifically focusing on its largest eigenvalue, and demonstrate that it conforms to a scaling limit characteristic of the critical phase in random matrix theory (specifically matching the Large Deviation Principle derived for Brownian motion at a sink). Furthermore, we identify several additional systems that obey identical asymptotic laws. By analyzing similar statistical patterns of rare occurrences spanning general stochastic matrices, financial options pricing, and neural network dynamics, we argue that critical RGM scaling provides a robust framework for describing global outlier statistics in outlier-prone systems.

Detailed analysis of the emitted photon statistics reveals distinct clustering characteristic of a sub-Poissonian distribution, thereby generating path-rotatable states through an appropriate selection of coupling geometries and topological arrangements to achieve maximum non-classical squeezing. Numerical and analytical work shows that, upon correct parameterization, the system supports single-photon non-classical behavior and extraordinary non-classical property levels (high non-classicality). Finally, the proposed setup is shown to afford, in an incoherent environment, high non-classical property levels and thus effective phase estimation sensitivity.

Although sparse high-dimensional data is frequently encountered in fields like genomics, traditional machine learning techniques typically lack either efficiency or precision when confronting massive datasets containing numerous covariates. We establish a universal lower limit on entropy production when control parameters are altered suddenly and return suddenly in any continuously driven quantum system designed to generate specific dynamics, assuming the initial state is thermal. The escalating crisis threatens our planet, prompting numerous research groups to focus on ecological issues and their associated technologies. To build this framework, we employ an Ecosystem Service Framework combined with the Plan-Do-Check-Action methodology, ensuring a thorough investigation of potential effects across all phases of the AI lifecycle. Findings indicate environment-boundary condition and the displacement of existing skill sets as the most critical risks. Domain generalization in Natural Language Processing aims to enable models trained on a specific source domain to perform effectively on unseen target domains. This capability is highly valuable for text classification, particularly in scenarios characterized by domain shift. Our work focuses on generalizing sign language events—extracting structured data from unstructured clinical text regarding the use of signed chemicals during anesthesia—from specialized domain sources to the broader target domain of general surgery sign language events. We adopt a "data poisoning" technique using obfuscation as a method to reduce the general model's bias toward any specific domain and prevent overfit, thereby enhancing true cross-domain capability. Specifically, we remove domain-specific terminologies from source domain texts to create poisons and apply these to pre-trained language models before fine-tuning for sign language event extraction, without accessing the target domain during training. Our evaluations indicate that applying such data poisoning to a base model is more efficient than removing those texts without the addition of an intermediate poisons step, resulting in a modest yet meaningful improvement in event extraction performance.

Dynamic planar fracture distinguishes itself from quasi-static fracture by producing remarkable wave radiants, high-energy dissipation, and exciting mechanical behaviors. This investigation numerically explores the interactions among material length, stiffness, and speed as they amplify distinct dynamic instability mechanisms. It begins by reviewing two prevalent phenomena: oscillatory instability, which generates oscillating radiants, and the tip-dividing instability, characterized in close proximity to branching radiants. It is then quantified the variation between the onset of these instabilities as a function of radiation, geometry, stiffness, and speed. Furthermore, it is advanced a refined phenomenological framework for tip-dividing dynamic instability that integrates material non-local effects with the energy release. The proposed model aligns closely with extensive simulation outcomes and offers superior agreement with existing experimental outcomes than earlier theoretical approaches. Ultimately, this refined formulation provides a valuable avenue for expanding the comprehension of dynamic structural failure.

This study examines communication over a finite-state channel (FSC) with feedback. We begin by presenting a regularity condition for the best achievable regularized information rate (RIR) in situations where current state awareness exists at both the encoder and decoder. We then offer an exponential rate of convergence to this optimal RIR value, assuming complete channel state non-causal knowledge. For scenarios without such assumption, we introduce a Markovian RIR formulation at the encoder that requires only feedback, establishing an suboptimal but achievable rate. We demonstrate that this value approaches optimality exponentially, dependent on neither concatenation nor feedback, without needing channel state estimation. However, this approach results in significant encoding complexity, which the paper mitigates by proposing another feedback-driven, achievable RIR value. This new suggestion represents a compromise between performance optimality and practical feasibility for real-world encoding.

Investigating a two-dimensional Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling, we find that attractive interactions combined with sufficiently strong spin-orbit coupling promote spin singlet superfluidity just below the band bottom. This phenomenon is confirmed by quantum entropy and finite-size scaling that aligns with mean-field predictions, indicating a number-conserving topological spin singlet state. Moreover, we discover this topological state can coexist with other phases, including spin triplet superfluidity, magnetic ordering, and a mixed spin singlet-triplet superfluid phase.

Hypergraph restoration functions as an innovative multivariate pattern completion technique capable of handling heterogeneous data characterized by diverse features and varying restoration dimensions, all while maintaining robustness against noise. Coordinating simultaneous observations across the Stochastic Astrophysical Project's multiple sites yields a rich dataset of richly diverse superluminous binary Ia systems. This paper explores a novel stochastic autoencoder (sAE) designed specifically for unsupervised learning and dimension reduction of time-series spectral data from Type Ia supernovae. The network successively reduces data dimensions and then reconstructs the original spectra. By integrating stochasticity directly into both degradation and reconstruction phases, the sAE can model probabilistic data distributions. Applied to Stochastic Astrophysical Project data, a specialized 2-layer sAE demonstrates effective dimension reduction by generating probabilistic latent representations. Furthermore, these probabilistic outputs facilitate the identification of optimal stochastic parameters through Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) theory: a Bayesian method employed in this study indicates that an ideal learning rate is roughly 0.001 and the optimal stochastic variance lies around 0.01. Traditional Federated Learning for audio requires manual labeling for all new categories across all client devices, a process that is time-consuming and costly, particularly given the frequent incorporation of novel, unlabeled classes in the wild. These outcomes demonstrate performance parity with a single neural model supporting both Turkish and English for sentiment and hate speech detection, all while relying solely on task depictions.

Achieving significantly better results in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) super-resolution is a major challenge, as it would enable extracting more comprehensive information from existing radar imagery. To address this, this paper introduces **MrSARP**, a hierarchical deep generative model designed to substantially improve SAR image super-resolution performance. Specifically, this approach is defined by a synergistic combination of two key innovations.

First, to overcome limitations where traditional methods struggle to generalize across diverse scenarios due to a scarcity of high-quality super-resolved training data, MrSARP utilizes **Bayesian-based sampling techniques** to synthesize a comprehensive dataset of super-resolved SAR images. These Bayesian-sampled images are then employed to train the model.

Second, to ensure the sustained generation of structurally coherent and realistic SAR textures during inference, a **Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** procedure is implemented. This mechanism effectively leverages the model's Bayesian parameters to refine the output.

Experimental evaluations on super-resolution tasks across images of distinct sizes and from the SAROAD dataset demonstrate that MrSARP achieves superior performance when compared against both conventional super-resolution techniques and existing deep learning methods.
